_comment: PLACEHOLDER — smoke-test content only, to validate the build pipeline end to end. This is NOT the Phase 2 prototype lesson. One chunk, one misconception, minimal question text. Physics stated here is correct but not yet run through the §32 Physics Accuracy Protocol at full lesson scope.
lessonTitle: Newton's Second Law: Force, Mass, and Acceleration
majorObjective: Analyze the relationship among net force, mass, and acceleration for an object.
subObjectives: State Newton's second law in words and symbolically.
Calculate net force, mass, or acceleration given the other two quantities.
Predict how acceleration changes when mass and/or net force change.
Interpret F-vs-a and F-vs-m graphs, including what the slope represents.

hook.prompt:
A constant net force $F$ acts on a cart of mass $m$, producing acceleration $a$. The cart is replaced with an otherwise identical cart of mass $2m$, and the same net force $F$ is applied.

What happens to the acceleration?
choices: It stays the same, because the force didn't change.
It becomes zero, because the cart is heavier.

priorKnowledge: Recall that acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and that force is a vector quantity with both magnitude and direction. You have already used $\vec{F}_{net} = \sum \vec{F}$ to combine multiple forces on an object.

chunks.title: Force, Mass, and Acceleration
chunks.concept:
Newton's second law states that the acceleration of an object is directly proportional to the net force acting on it and inversely proportional to its mass: $\vec{a} = \vec{F}_{net} / m$, usually written $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$.

This is a relationship between three quantities, not a formula to substitute into blindly — before using it, identify the system, identify every force acting on it, and find the net force first.
chunks.representation: Free-body diagram: draw every force acting on the object as an arrow from its center, then find $\vec{F}_{net}$ by vector addition before applying $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$.

steps: Known: m = 2.0 kg, F_net = 6.0 N (horizontal, rightward).
Assumption: frictionless track, force is constant.
Representation: free-body diagram shows only the 6.0 N applied force horizontally (gravity and normal force cancel vertically).
Check direction: positive, so acceleration points rightward, same direction as F_net.
Reasonableness: a modest force on a few-kilogram cart giving a few m/s² is physically sensible.

formativeCheck.question: If the net force on an object triples while its mass stays the same, what happens to its acceleration?
choices: It is cut to a third.
It increases by a factor of 9.

feedback.correct: Correct — with mass constant, a ∝ F_net, so tripling the net force triples the acceleration.

incorrect.1: Acceleration only stays constant if force and mass change in the same proportion — here only force changed.
incorrect.2: This inverts the relationship. Increasing net force increases acceleration, it doesn't reduce it.
incorrect.3: That would be true for something proportional to F², but Newton's second law is linear in F_net.

hint: Hold mass fixed in F_net = ma and ask what happens to a as F_net changes.
formativeCheck.solution: a = F_net / m. Tripling F_net with m unchanged triples a.

interactiveComponent.description: Use the sliders to vary mass and net force independently and observe the resulting acceleration, the F-vs-a graph, and the F-vs-m graph. Before moving a slider, predict what will happen.

misconceptions.statement: A heavier object requires a proportionally larger force just to keep it moving at constant velocity.
misconceptions.diagnostic: A 10 kg block and a 2 kg block both slide at constant velocity across a frictionless floor. Does the 10 kg block need a larger applied force to keep moving?
misconceptions.correction: At constant velocity, acceleration is zero, so by Newton's second law the *net* force is zero regardless of mass — on a frictionless surface, no applied force is needed at all to maintain constant velocity. Mass affects how hard it is to *change* an object's velocity (inertia), not what force is needed to sustain a constant one.

representationConnections: The same relationship $F_{net} = ma$ appears as: a linear F-vs-a graph (slope = m) when mass is fixed; a linear F-vs-m graph (slope = a) when acceleration is fixed; a free-body diagram whose vector sum gives F_net; and the verbal statement that acceleration is proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass.
apIbConnection: AP Physics 1 Free-Response questions frequently ask you to justify a claim about acceleration using Newton's second law in words, not just algebra — practice stating *why* a ∝ F_net and a ∝ 1/m, not just the equation.
summary: Newton's second law, $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$, relates net force, mass, and acceleration. Acceleration is proportional to net force and inversely proportional to mass. Always find the net force from a free-body diagram before applying the law.

exitQuestion.question: A student plots net force on the y-axis against acceleration on the x-axis for a single object of unknown mass and gets a straight line through the origin. What does the slope of this line represent?

feedback.correct: Correct — F_net = ma means F_net vs a is linear with slope m, so the slope directly gives the object's mass.

incorrect.1: Weight is mg, a force — it isn't what this particular slope represents; the axes here are F_net and a, not F_net and g.
incorrect.2: Acceleration is already one of the plotted axes, not the slope of the line.
incorrect.3: Nothing in this graph involves a normal force or friction — there's no basis to extract a friction coefficient here.

hint: Compare F_net = ma to the general line equation y = (slope)·x.
exitQuestion.solution: Matching F_net = m·a to y = (slope)·x shows slope = m.
